content: The association of mass treatment with azithromycin in trachoma-endemic communities has been linked to a short-term reduction in the risk of diarrhea among young children. This finding was published in the American Journal of Tropical Medicine and Hygiene in 2011. A study conducted in Tanzania demonstrated that a single dose of azithromycin during mass drug administration for trachoma led to a short-term reduction in malaria. This was reported in the journal Emerging Infectious Diseases in 2014. The Grading of Recommendations, Assessment, Development, and Evaluation (GRADE) handbook, published in 2013, was used to guide the formulation of recommendations for the mass administration of azithromycin to children under five years of age to promote child survival. This process included evaluating intervention effects, values, resources, equity, acceptability, and feasibility. The WHO Guideline Development Group (GDG) conducted scoping and prioritization of outcomes, and evidence-informed recommendations were finalized during a meeting in Geneva in early 2019. Sixteen external experts reviewed the preliminary version of the guideline. The WHO commissioned three systematic reviews to synthesize evidence on the efficacy of mass drug administration (MDA) with azithromycin, antimicrobial resistance (AMR), adverse effects, dosing regimens, and mechanisms of action. The GDG concluded that the three randomized controlled trials (RCTs) evaluating MDA-azithromycin's effect on mortality differed significantly in design, precluding simple pooling of results. Two of the RCTs showed a statistically significant reduction in all-cause mortality among those randomized to MDA-azithromycin. However, the third trial, which combined MDA-azithromycin with seasonal malaria chemoprophylaxis (SMC), did not show a reduction in the composite outcome of hospitalization or mortality compared to SMC alone. All studies reporting mortality benefits from MDA-azithromycin were conducted in sub-Saharan African countries with high under-five child mortality rates in malaria-endemic areas. The studies did not find reductions in acute respiratory tract infections, malaria, or hospitalizations. However, two RCTs showed a significant reduction in diarrhea incidence among children receiving MDA-azithromycin. Some studies have demonstrated considerable resistance of fecal and nasopharyngeal flora to macrolide antibiotics in children receiving MDA-azithromycin. It remains unclear whether prolonged MDA-azithromycin use to improve childhood mortality would increase the circulation of resistant strains in the population. The clinical implications of these changes are not well understood. The adverse effects of azithromycin are primarily gastrointestinal, including diarrhea, vomiting, abdominal pain, and nausea. Infants may be at increased risk of developing pyloric stenosis, particularly in the first month of life. After weighing the benefits and potential harms of the intervention, along with the values and preferences of the target population, the GDG made two recommendations regarding MDA-azithromycin implementation. The first recommendation advises against the universal use of MDA-azithromycin as a child survival intervention in lowand middle-income countries (LMICs), citing low-quality evidence. The second recommendation suggests considering MDA-azithromycin for children aged 1 to 11 months in sub-Saharan African settings with high infant and under-five mortality rates, provided that mortality rates, adverse effects, and AMR are continuously monitored, and existing child survival interventions are concurrently strengthened. The suggested MDA-azithromycin regimen is 20 mg/kg oral azithromycin as a single dose every six months. Additional research is needed to confirm the optimal dose, frequency, and number of intervention cycles. If MDA-azithromycin is provided as part of trachoma prevention programs, infants in target populations would require only one additional dose per year. The US FDA, UK Medicines Regulatory Agency, Health Canada, and Australia's Therapeutic Goods Administration approve azithromycin use in children for several conditions but note a lack of safety and efficacy data in children under six months. Pharmacovigilance is essential in this age group. In settings with low SMC coverage, scaling up SMC should take precedence over MDA-azithromycin implementation. Local consultation to confirm acceptability and preferences is crucial when planning implementation. The recommendation is applicable for 2–3 years, after which the guidelines are expected to be updated with new evidence. The GDG emphasized the need for continuous monitoring of infant and child mortality, AMR, and pharmacovigilance. They also recommended strengthening other ongoing child survival interventions concurrently. Plans for updating the guideline include reviewing additional MDA-azithromycin data from large ongoing studies and planned research investments. In 2018, 3 million children under five years of age died, with most deaths occurring in low-income countries, particularly in sub-Saharan Africa. Sustainable Development Goal 3 aims to end preventable deaths of newborns and children under five by 2030, necessitating simple, feasible, and cost-effective interventions to reduce deaths from pneumonia, diarrhea, and malaria in LMICs. MDA-azithromycin has been effective in controlling neglected tropical diseases such as trachoma, filariasis, schistosomiasis, and onchocerciasis. Azithromycin is also effective in treating acute lower respiratory tract and enteric infections. However, the exact mechanisms by which MDA-azithromycin reduces child mortality remain unclear.
